title: How Grassoline Works
summary: An early HowStuffWorks-era episode in which Josh Clark and editor Chris Pallette discuss the article "Can We Fuel Cars with Grass?" Switch grass is presented as a cellulosic ethanol feedstock that can grow on marginal land where it can improve soil over about a dozen years, unlike corn or sugarcane that compete with food. They also cover the carbon debt from converting rainforest to biofuel crops (citing a New Scientist article), palm oil in Indonesia, and the argument that domestic energy supplies could reduce conflict over oil. The episode is short and the transcript is partly garbled by captioning errors.

entities.name: Can We Fuel Cars with Grass?

segments.title: Opening sponsor read and greeting
segments.summary: A sponsor read for a Camry opens the episode, followed by the greeting and introduction of Josh Clark and editor Chris Pallette.

segments.title: Switch grass as a cellulosic biofuel feedstock
segments.summary: Chris Pallette summarizes the article: switch grass can be a cellulose source for biofuel, unlike corn or sugarcane that are food crops, and it could be grown on marginal land where crops are not practical.

segments.title: Soil improvement and what switch grass is
segments.summary: The hosts say switch grass improves soil so that scrubland can become farmland after about a dozen years, and they describe it as a grass often viewed as weedy or invasive, with some ornamental types.

segments.title: Carbon debt from converting land to biofuel crops
segments.summary: Chris cites a New Scientist report that converting Brazilian rainforest to biofuel crops could release large amounts of carbon dioxide, so biofuels may need years to recoup that carbon debt. Josh notes that switch grass is not the only option, since palm oil is grown in Indonesia.

segments.title: Energy self-sufficiency, oil and war, and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts argue that energy self-sufficiency could reduce regional conflict over oil, then Josh directs listeners to the article and the sign-off repeats a sponsor read.
